lessons.title: Designing a Drip Irrigation System
lessons.body: A drip system saves water and labour, but you must design it for your plot. Start by measuring your field: 1 hectare is 100 m by 100 m. For vegetables, use drip lines spaced 30â50 cm apart, with emitters every 20â30 cm. If you grow tomatoes on 1 m beds, you need about 10,000 m of drip line per hectare. Calculate water needs: each plant needs 2â4 litres per day. With 20,000 plants, that's 40,000â80,000 litres daily. A pump delivering 10,000 litres per hour can run for 4â8 hours. Choose a pump size: for a 1-hectare field, a 1.5â2 HP pump with a flow of 10â20 mÂ³/h is typical. You also need a filter (screen or sand) to prevent clogging, a pressure regulator (1â1.5 bar), and a mainline (50â63 mm PVC) and sub-mainlines (32â40 mm). Lay drip lines along the beds. Use connectors and end caps. In Africa, many farmers use gravity-fed systems from a tank on a 2â3 m stand; that gives about 0.2â0.3 bar, enough for short runs. For larger fields, use a solar pump. Cost: a basic kit for 1 hectare costs $800â$1,500. You can start with a smaller area and expand. Always install a valve for each section so you can water different crops separately. Test the system for even emission. Remember: drip irrigation reduces water use by 30â50% compared to furrow. It also reduces weeds and diseases. But you must maintain it. Design for easy flushing: put flush valves at the end of each drip line. If your water is dirty, use a settling tank before the filter. Plan your layout on paper first. Mark the position of the pump, tank, mainlines, and beds. This saves time and money.

lessons.title: Scheduling Irrigation Based on Crop Needs
lessons.body: Crops need different amounts of water at different stages. For tomatoes, water 2â4 litres per plant per day during fruiting, but only 1â2 litres during early growth. For leafy greens like kale, 2â3 litres per plant per day. For onions, 1â2 litres. The key is to check soil moisture before watering. Stick your finger 10 cm into the soil. If it feels dry, irrigate. If it's moist, wait. A simple tool is a tensiometer, but you can also use a shovel to dig a small hole and feel the soil. In sandy soil, water drains quickly, so you may need to irrigate daily. In clay soil, water stays longer, so every 2â3 days. A good rule: irrigate when the soil moisture drops to 50% of field capacity. For drip, run the system for 1â2 hours per day, depending on flow rate. If each emitter gives 2 litres per hour, and you have 20,000 emitters, you deliver 40,000 litres in 1 hour. That's enough for 1 hectare of tomatoes. But in hot weather, increase to 1.5â2 hours. In cool weather, reduce. Use a simple schedule: early morning (6â8 am) is best because less evaporation. Avoid evening watering to prevent fungal diseases. Also, check the weather forecast: if rain is expected, skip irrigation. You can use a rain gauge or just a tin can. Keep a record of when you irrigate and how much. After a week, adjust. For example, if plants look wilted in the afternoon, they need more water. If leaves turn yellow and soil is soggy, you are overwatering. A cheap moisture meter costs $10â$20. It saves water and improves yields. Remember: overwatering leaches nutrients and causes root rot. Underwatering stresses plants and reduces yield. So schedule based on crop, soil, and weather.

lessons.title: Rainwater Harvesting and Storage
lessons.body: In many parts of Africa, rain is seasonal. You can harvest rainwater from roofs or from the ground. For a 1-hectare farm, you need storage for dry spells. A simple method: dig a pond lined with clay or plastic. A pond of 10 m x 10 m x 2 m deep holds 200,000 litres. That can irrigate 1 hectare for 2â3 days. But you can also use tanks. A 5,000-litre tank costs $500â$800. To fill it, you need a roof area of about 100 mÂ² with 50 mm of rain. That's common in a single storm. So harvest from your house, shed, or a small shelter. Use gutters and a first-flush diverter to keep out leaves and dirt. For field-scale, build a check dam or a small reservoir. In dry areas, use a sand dam: build a concrete wall across a seasonal riverbed, and sand accumulates behind it. Water is stored in the sand and can be extracted with a well. Another method: contour ridges and tied ridges to capture runoff in the field. For storage, a lined pond with a plastic liner (0.5 mm thick) costs about $2â$3 per mÂ². A 200 mÂ² pond costs $400â$600. Cover the pond to reduce evaporation: use a shade net or floating balls. Evaporation can lose 5â10 mm per day. That's 1,000â2,000 litres per day from a 200 mÂ² pond. So cover it. Also, keep the water clean: use a filter before drip irrigation. You can also harvest rainwater from the drip system's runoff? No, drip doesn't produce runoff. But you can direct roof water to a tank, then use a pump to the drip system. A solar pump (200 W) can lift water from a tank to a 2 m high tank for gravity feed. Cost: $200â$400. Start small: a 1,000-litre tank for a nursery. Then scale up. Rainwater harvesting reduces your water bill and gives you control.

lessons.title: Using Mulch to Conserve Moisture
lessons.body: Mulch is any material you spread on the soil surface to reduce evaporation. In Africa, you can use dry grass, straw, maize stover, banana leaves, or plastic mulch. Organic mulch: spread a layer 5â10 cm thick around plants. It keeps soil moist, suppresses weeds, and adds organic matter. For example, in a tomato field, apply mulch after transplanting. You need about 2â3 tonnes of dry grass per hectare. That's a lot, but you can collect from nearby fields. Plastic mulch: use black or silver plastic film. It warms soil, prevents weeds, and saves water. A roll of 1.2 m wide plastic covers about 100 m of bed. Cost: $30â$50 per roll. You need about 100 rolls for 1 hectare if beds are 1 m apart. That's $3,000â$5,000, which is expensive. But it lasts 2â3 seasons if you handle it carefully. Organic mulch is cheaper but breaks down. You can also use living mulch: plant cover crops like cowpea or sweet potato between rows. They shade the soil and reduce evaporation. But they compete for water, so only use in rainy season. The best mulch for water conservation is a combination: organic mulch under the plants, and plastic on the paths? No, keep it simple. For a 1-hectare vegetable farm, start with organic mulch on half the field and compare. You will see that mulched soil stays moist 2â3 days longer. That means you can irrigate every 3 days instead of every day. You save 30â50% water. Also, mulch keeps soil temperature stable, which helps roots. Apply mulch after rain or irrigation, when soil is wet. Don't put mulch right against the stem; leave a small gap to prevent rot. Reapply as it decomposes. In dry areas, mulch is essential. It is one of the cheapest ways to improve water use. Use what you have: grass, leaves, crop residues. Avoid mulching with fresh manure or hay that has seeds. Always test a small area first.

lessons.title: Monitoring Soil Moisture with Sensors
lessons.body: You don't need expensive tools to monitor soil moisture. But sensors give you accurate data. The cheapest is a tensiometer: a tube with a ceramic tip and a gauge. It measures how hard plants must work to extract water. Cost: $30â$80. Place tensiometers at 20 cm and 40 cm depth. When the reading is above 50 centibars (cb), it's time to irrigate. For sandy soil, irrigate at 30 cb; for clay, at 60 cb. Another tool: a capacitance probe or a handheld moisture meter. These cost $50â$200. They give a percentage reading. You can also use a simple gypsum block, but it degrades. For a 1-hectare farm, you need at least 3â5 sensors at different points. If you can't afford sensors, use the feel method: squeeze soil in your hand. If it forms a ball and leaves a slight moisture on your palm, it's fine. If it crumbles, it's dry. If it drips, it's too wet. You can also use a shovel to check. But sensors save water and time. For drip irrigation, you can automate with a controller that reads sensors. A basic controller costs $100â$200. It turns the pump on when soil moisture drops below a set point. That saves water and labour. In Africa, you can use a smartphone app like 'Soil Moisture' or 'Irrigation Manager' to log readings. But you need a sensor that connects via Bluetooth. Some farmers use a simple tensiometer and check it daily. That's enough. Keep a record: date, reading, and action. After a season, you will know your soil's behaviour. Remember: sensors must be installed correctly. Insert them in the root zone, not on the surface. Avoid areas that are too wet or dry. Calibrate them according to the manufacturer. If you use a tensiometer, refill it with distilled water and remove air bubbles. A well-monitored system uses 20â30% less water. So the investment pays back in one season.

lessons.title: Maintaining Irrigation Lines and Emitters
lessons.body: Drip irrigation clogs easily. You must maintain it weekly. First, flush the lines. Open the end caps of each drip line and let water run for 2â3 minutes. Do this every week. This removes sediment and roots. Second, clean the filter. If you have a screen filter, remove the screen and rinse it. If it's a sand filter, backwash it. Do this daily if water is dirty. Third, check emitters. Walk along the lines and look for dry spots or gushers. A clogged emitter shows no water; a broken one shows a jet. Replace clogged emitters with a goof plug or a new emitter. You can also use a needle to clean the emitter, but be careful not to damage it. Fourth, use acid treatment. Once a month, inject a small amount of hydrochloric acid (0.5%) or vinegar to dissolve mineral deposits. But be careful: wear gloves and goggles. For organic matter, use chlorine (1â2 ppm) once a month. Fifth, check pressure. Use a pressure gauge at the end of the mainline. If pressure drops, there is a leak or clog. Fix leaks with tape or new connectors. Sixth, store drip lines properly during off-season. Remove them, clean them, and hang them in a shed. Don't leave them in the sun. UV light damages plastic. Seventh, protect against rodents. Mice and rats chew drip lines. Use traps or keep the field clean. Eighth, train your workers. Show them how to flush and check emitters. A simple maintenance schedule: daily: check filter and pressure. Weekly: flush lines and check emitters. Monthly: acid or chlorine treatment. Yearly: replace damaged lines. If you maintain well, a drip system lasts 5â10 years. If not, it clogs in one season. So spend 30 minutes per day on maintenance. It saves water, money, and crops.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Water Management & Irrigation for One Hectare

Water is the single largest controllable input in a one-hectare vegetable enterprise â and the one most often wasted. On a well-managed hectare of drip-irrigated tomatoes, onions, or kale, water costs can run 8â15% of total variable costs. On a poorly managed hectare using flood or overhead irrigation, that figure can double, and yields can fall 30â50% through waterlogging, disease, and leaching of the fertiliser you paid for.

This module gives you the practical numbers, design rules, and maintenance routines to run a profitable one-hectare vegetable block. It is written for the African smallholder and emerging commercial grower: limited capital, unreliable grid power, seasonal rainfall, and a market that pays for quality and consistency. Every recommendation here is chosen because it pays back within one or two seasons.

Designing a Drip Irrigation System for One Hectare

Design starts with the crop, not the pipe. A hectare of tomatoes at 1.0 m Ã 0.4 m spacing has roughly 25,000 plants. At peak demand, each plant needs 2â4 litres per day. That is 50,000â100,000 litres (50â100 mÂ³) per day â the number that determines your pump, tank, and pipe sizes.

Rules of thumb for a one-hectare drip block in Africa:

  • Emitter flow: 2 L/h for sandy soils (wets a wider bulb faster), 4 L/h for heavy clay loams.
  • Emitter spacing: 30 cm for vegetables, 20 cm for lettuce and herbs.
  • Lateral spacing: match row spacing â 0.9â1.2 m for most vegetables.
  • Lateral length: keep below 60 m on flat ground to maintain pressure uniformity above 90%.
  • Filtration: 120-mesh screen filter minimum; 200-mesh if using surface water or fertigation.
  • Pump sizing: assume 2 bar operating pressure at the filter outlet plus friction losses.

Table 1: Peak Daily Water Requirement by Crop (1 Hectare)

Crop Season length Peak demand (mÂ³/day/ha) Total season water (mÂ³) Approx. water cost @ US$0.30/mÂ³
Tomato (open field)120 days60â805,000â6,500US$1,500â1,950
Onion130 days45â604,000â5,000US$1,200â1,500
Kale / collards90 days40â552,800â3,500US$840â1,050
French beans75 days45â602,500â3,200US$750â960
Watermelon100 days55â754,000â5,200US$1,200â1,560

Source: FAO Crop Water Information Sheets (AquaCrop / CROPWAT), fao.org/land-water/databases-and-software/crop-information. Costs are illustrative; adjust for local water tariff or pumping cost.

Scheduling Irrigation Based on Crop Needs

Do not irrigate on a fixed calendar. Irrigate when the crop needs it. The practical method for a one-hectare block is the checkbook method: track daily crop water use (ETc) and rainfall, and refill the soil when the deficit reaches your allowable depletion.

ETc = ETo Ã Kc, where ETo is reference evapotranspiration (available free from FAO's CROPWAT or national meteorological services) and Kc is the crop coefficient. For tomatoes at mid-season, Kc â 1.15. If ETo = 5 mm/day, ETc = 5.75 mm/day. One hectare needs 57.5 mÂ³ of water per day â matching the table above.

Run drip for the number of hours needed to replace that deficit. A 1-hectare block with 25,000 emitters at 2 L/h delivers 50,000 L/h = 50 mÂ³/h. To apply 57.5 mÂ³, run the system for about 1 hour 10 minutes. Split into two sessions (early morning and late afternoon) on very hot days to reduce evaporation and heat stress.

Table 2: Irrigation Scheduling Quick Reference

Soil type Allowable depletion (% of available water) Irrigate when deficit reaches Typical interval (mid-season)
Sandy40â50%12â15 mmEvery 1â2 days
Sandy loam50%18â22 mmEvery 2â3 days
Loam50â60%25â30 mmEvery 3â4 days
Clay loam55â65%30â35 mmEvery 4â5 days
Clay60%35â40 mmEvery 5â7 days

Source: FAO Irrigation & Drainage Paper 56, Crop Evapotranspiration (Allen et al., 1998), fao.org/3/x0490e/x0490e00.htm. Values assume effective rooting depth of 30â60 cm for vegetables.

Rainwater Harvesting and Storage

In most of sub-Saharan Africa, a 1-hectare vegetable block receives 600â1,200 mm of rain per year â but in 2â3 heavy events. Capturing even 10% of that on a 1,000 mÂ² roof or runoff catchment yields 60â120 mÂ³ per year: enough to cover 15â25% of your dry-season irrigation. A 10,000-litre tank (US$400â800 installed) pays back in one season at a water cost of US$0.30/mÂ³.

Practical rules: line earth dams and ponds with 1.0 mm HDPE geomembrane; cover tanks to reduce evaporation and mosquito breeding; install a first-flush diverter to keep silt and bird droppings out of the tank.

Using Mulch to Conserve Moisture

Organic mulch (crop residue, grass, straw) 5â10 cm thick cuts evaporation from the soil surface by 30â50% and suppresses weeds. On a one-hectare tomato block, mulching can save 800â1,200 mÂ³ of water per season â worth US$240â360 in water cost alone, before counting labour savings on weeding. Black plastic mulch is more expensive (US$300â500/ha) but warms soil, reduces disease splash, and is common in commercial tomato and pepper production. Biodegradable mulch films now cost within 15% of conventional plastic and avoid disposal problems.

Monitoring Soil Moisture with Sensors

You do not need expensive equipment. A US$15â40 tensiometer or a US$20 capacitance probe at 20 cm and 40 cm depth tells you when to irrigate and when to stop. Read them every morning at the same time. Target range for vegetables: 20â40 kPa (tensiometer) in sandy soils, 30â50 kPa in loams. If you cannot afford sensors, use the feel and appearance method: squeeze a handful of soil from 20 cm depth. If it forms a ball that crumbles easily, irrigate soon. If it drips, stop.

â  SAFETY WARNING â ELECTRICAL AND WATER HAZARDS

Never install or service a pump, controller, or sensor wiring while it is connected to power. Use a qualified electrician for all mains connections, and fit an earth-leakage circuit breaker (ELCB/RCD). Solar pump wiring can still deliver lethal DC voltage â disconnect panels before working on cables. Keep all electrical joints at least 60 cm above ground and inside IP65 enclosures. Do not enter a wet pump house or tank alone. If using surface water, treat it and wear gloves when cleaning filters â contaminated water can carry cholera, typhoid, and bilharzia. Never mix concentrated fertiliser with untreated surface water in an open tank; use a covered fertigation tank and follow the label.

Maintaining Irrigation Lines and Emitters

Clogged emitters are the number one cause of drip system failure in Africa. Chlorine, iron, and calcium in borehole water, plus algae in surface water, block emitters within weeks if not managed. Maintenance schedule:

  • Weekly: flush lateral ends for 2 minutes; clean the screen filter.
  • Monthly: inject chlorine (1â2 ppm free chlorine) for 30 minutes; check emitter flow in 5 random spots.
  • Seasonally: acid-treat with 1% hydrochloric or citric acid to dissolve calcium; replace damaged laterals.
  • Annually: replace filter cartridges, check pump seals, and test pressure at the farthest emitter.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Know your peak daily water demand in mÂ³ before you buy a pump or tank.
  2. Install a 120-mesh filter and flush it weekly â no exceptions.
  3. Schedule by ETc, not by calendar; adjust after every rain event.
  4. Use a tensiometer or feel test to confirm soil moisture before irrigating.
  5. Mulch every bed to cut evaporation 30â50% and suppress weeds.
  6. Harvest and store rainwater in covered, lined tanks with first-flush diversion.
  7. Chlorinate lines monthly and acid-treat seasonally to prevent emitter clogging.
  8. Keep a simple log: date, hours run, rainfall, and any emitter issues.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • FAO Irrigation & Drainage Paper 56 â Crop Evapotranspiration: fao.org/3/x0490e/x0490e00.htm
  • FAO â Sprinkler and Trickle Irrigation Systems (Paper 66): fao.org/3/s8684e/s8684e00.htm
  • FAO Land & Water â Crop Information and CROPWAT software: fao.org/land-water/databases-and-software/crop-information
  • IWMI â Water for Food, Water for Life (open access): iwmi.cgiar.org
  • AGRA â Africa Agriculture Status Report (irrigation chapters): agra.org

Business bottom line: On a one-hectare vegetable block in Africa, moving from flood to scheduled drip irrigation typically cuts water use 40â60%, cuts labour for irrigation 70%, and lifts marketable yield 20â35%. The capital cost (US$1,200â2,500 for a 1-ha drip kit) is recovered in one to two seasons. The maintenance habits in this module â filters, flushing, sensors, mulch â are what protect that investment.

quiz.q: What is the typical spacing for drip lines in a vegetable field?
quiz.explanation: Drip lines are usually spaced 30-50 cm apart for vegetables to ensure water reaches the root zone.

quiz.q: How many litres of water does a tomato plant need per day during fruiting?
quiz.explanation: Tomatoes in fruiting stage require 2-4 litres per plant per day for optimal yield.

quiz.q: What is the recommended pressure for a drip irrigation system?
quiz.explanation: Most drip systems operate best at 1-1.5 bar pressure to ensure even emitter flow.

quiz.q: Which component prevents clogging in a drip system?
quiz.explanation: A filter removes sediment and debris that can clog emitters.

quiz.q: What is the best time of day to irrigate?
quiz.explanation: Early morning irrigation reduces evaporation and prevents fungal diseases.

quiz.q: How deep should you check soil moisture with your finger?
quiz.explanation: Checking at 10 cm depth gives a good indication of moisture in the root zone.

quiz.q: What is a tensiometer used for?
quiz.explanation: A tensiometer measures how tightly soil holds water, indicating when to irrigate.

quiz.q: At what tensiometer reading should you irrigate sandy soil?
quiz.explanation: Sandy soil should be irrigated at around 30 centibars to avoid water stress.

quiz.q: What is the water holding capacity of a 10m x 10m x 2m pond?
quiz.explanation: Volume = 10 x 10 x 2 = 200 cubic meters = 200,000 litres.

quiz.q: How much roof area is needed to collect 5,000 litres from 50 mm of rain?
quiz.explanation: 50 mm rain on 100 mÂ² gives 5,000 litres (100 x 0.05 = 5 mÂ³ = 5,000 L).

quiz.q: What is a first-flush diverter used for?
options: B) To remove debris from first rainwater
quiz.explanation: It discards the first dirty rainwater to keep storage clean.

quiz.q: What is a sand dam?
options: A) A dam made of sand
B) A concrete wall across a riverbed to store water in sand
quiz.explanation: A sand dam traps sand and water in seasonal riverbeds, providing stored water.

quiz.q: How much water can evaporate from an uncovered pond per day?
quiz.explanation: Evaporation from open water in hot climates is typically 5-10 mm per day.

quiz.q: What is the recommended thickness for organic mulch?
quiz.explanation: A 5-10 cm layer of organic mulch effectively reduces evaporation and suppresses weeds.

quiz.q: Which mulch is best for warming soil?
quiz.explanation: Black plastic mulch absorbs heat and warms the soil, benefiting warm-season crops.

quiz.q: How much water can mulch save?
quiz.explanation: Mulch can reduce irrigation water use by 30-50% by reducing evaporation.

quiz.q: What is a living mulch?
quiz.explanation: Living mulch is a cover crop that shades soil and conserves moisture.

quiz.q: How often should you flush drip lines?
quiz.explanation: Weekly flushing removes sediment and prevents clogging.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of acid treatment in drip lines?
quiz.explanation: Acid dissolves calcium and other mineral deposits that clog emitters.

quiz.q: What concentration of chlorine is used for organic matter control?
quiz.explanation: 1-2 ppm chlorine controls organic matter without harming plants.

quiz.q: How long should you flush each drip line?
quiz.explanation: Flushing for 2-3 minutes clears accumulated debris.

quiz.q: What causes a gusher in a drip line?
quiz.explanation: A broken emitter allows a continuous stream, called a gusher.

quiz.q: What is a goof plug used for?
options: B) To plug a clogged emitter hole
quiz.explanation: A goof plug seals an emitter hole that is no longer needed.

quiz.q: How often should you check the filter?
quiz.explanation: Filters should be checked daily, especially with dirty water.

quiz.q: What is the minimum number of sensors for a 1-hectare field?
quiz.explanation: 3-5 sensors at different points give a representative picture of soil moisture.

quiz.q: What does a capacitance probe measure?
quiz.explanation: Capacitance probes measure soil moisture by detecting dielectric constant.

quiz.q: What is the feel method for checking soil moisture?
quiz.explanation: Squeezing soil and observing how it holds together indicates moisture level.

quiz.q: What is the recommended depth for installing tensiometers?
quiz.explanation: Tensiometers at 20 cm and 40 cm cover the main root zone for vegetables.

quiz.q: How much water can a well-monitored system save?
quiz.explanation: Proper monitoring reduces water use by 20-30% compared to fixed schedules.

quiz.q: What is the lifespan of a well-maintained drip system?
quiz.explanation: With proper maintenance, drip lines last 5-10 years.
